title: Finding Collaborators
answer: This page covers the practical work of locating and assessing research partners for AI grant proposals, from scanning published work and model repositories to checking institutional and disciplinary fit. It is aimed at a researcher or research manager who needs to build a credible team around a specific funding call, not at a machine learning engineer tuning a recommender system. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the practical work of locating and assessing research partners for AI grant proposals, from scanning published work and model repositories to checking institutional and disciplinary fit. It is aimed at a researcher or research manager who needs to build a credible team around a specific funding call, not at a machine learning engineer tuning a recommender system. The focus is on evidence of past work, such as papers, extracted claims, models, and tools, rather than on personal networks alone.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The collaborator search draws on the site's structured research library, which currently holds 135 research papers, 10,555 extracted claims, 801 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 674 glossary terms. These records are indexed by field and method, so a search for a topic returns not only paper titles but also the specific claims, models, and tools associated with each author. The site links to the original paper rather than to a third-party search tool, which keeps the underlying source material directly accessible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A researcher typically starts with the topic of a funding call, searches the library for related papers and extracted claims, and then follows author names and institutional affiliations to build a shortlist. They compare each candidate's recent models and tools against the proposal's technical needs, looking for complementary skills rather than overlapping ones. The work is iterative: a promising paper leads to its authors, whose other papers and tools are then checked for consistency and relevance, and the shortlist is narrowed by practical constraints such as location, eligibility, and past collaboration patterns.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because a collaborator's track record is only as good as the underlying papers and claims. The site links to original papers rather than a third-party search tool, so a researcher can check authorship order, funding disclosures, and retraction status directly. Risks include mistaking a model's listed contributor for the corresponding author, or relying on an extracted claim that has been taken out of context. There is no automated vetting of a person's suitability, so the responsibility for verifying identity, affiliation, and conflict of interest remains with the person assembling the proposal team.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more structured matching, linking authors to their models, tools, and funding histories so that a proposal team can be assembled from evidence rather than memory. As the library grows, expect finer-grained filters for methodological fit and geographic or institutional eligibility, and possibly alerts when a researcher's new work matches an open call. The underlying challenge is not finding more names but reducing the time spent verifying that a potential collaborator's past work actually supports the role they would play in a grant.
